articles.title: A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked
articles.author: Andrew Cullen, Guest Research Fellow, School of Computing and Information Systems, The University of Melbourne
paras: Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.
The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.

PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.

The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.
PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it.

In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase.
The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet.
Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web.
Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix.
In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit.
This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready.
Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule.

Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix.
Why does this keep happening?
Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding.

Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data.

Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital.
Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is.

This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security.

For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days.
Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning.
Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call.

Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on.

Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening.
Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.

articles.title: Protest as a pillar of democracy
articles.author: Malka Older
paras: Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have
Originally published on Global Voices

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings. Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.

But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that. Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.

Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have. With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.

Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action. Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement. One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy. In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.

Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out. Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.

That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are. And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression. Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa. This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia. And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.

As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad. The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability. And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

As with all our monthly spotlights, this one is in many ways about showing the common threads that link all of our countries, as well as the exceptions that can open us to new ideas or inspire us to a different kind of action. This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.

articles.title: Palestine is already living under the Big Tech authoritarianism the world is being sold
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control
Originally published on Global Voices
An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025. Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction. Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.

Surveillance, data harvesting, facial recognition, telecommunications blackouts, digital censorship and algorithmic systems are now woven into this architecture of control. The genocidal war on Gaza has exposed the consequences with devastating clarity, where technologies built to collect, process and classify information have been absorbed into systems that surveil, target and kill Palestinians.

But Palestine is also a warning about what comes next. Technologies developed, tested and refined under occupation do not stay there. They become products, expertise and business models that circulate globally. What emerges is a political economy in which military and intelligence institutions, technology companies, investors and governments converge around the extraction and processing of data as a means of exercising power.

This is one of the central arguments of Digital Domination, a publication of The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media’s Maryam Abu Daqqa Fellowship, which brings together five studies on artificial intelligence, surveillance, data extraction and corporate power in Palestine and beyond. The fellowship is named after Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian journalist murdered by Israel in Gaza in August 2025 while documenting life under siege. Across different cases, the research points to the same transformation, showing how emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control. It is becoming their infrastructure.

Israel’s surveillance industry shows this plainly. It operates through intimate ties between military and intelligence institutions, private companies, venture capital and international markets. Tools tested on Palestinians are refined, repackaged as commercial products and exported to the world as security solutions. This is no accident of a thriving tech sector. It is a political and economic system in which security technologies gain value precisely because of their capacity to monitor, classify and control populations.

The violence these systems enable is increasingly literal. Investigations into Israel’s AI-assisted targeting systems, including Lavender, The Gospel and Where’s Daddy, have documented how machine-learning systems and mass surveillance data have been folded into the identification and targeting of Palestinians in Gaza.

A new film, NAZA, produced by The Guardian and built on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, details the secret systems used to select people for bombing in their homes at night, in the knowledge that their families would be killed, too. At a military conference in London in late June, an executive from the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems presented a slide crediting its digital command system with 850,000 “real-time intel targets” across Gaza and Lebanon between October 2023 and the end of 2025. The company has since tried to recast the figure as aggregate system activity, a claim that sits uneasily with the slide itself.

The significance is not that an algorithm has replaced human violence. It is that these systems increase the scale, speed and bureaucratic distance at which violence is organised, while cloaking life-and-death decisions in the appearance of technical objectivity. In June, Amnesty International and more than 100 other signatories warned that systems such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy dilute human responsibility and obscure international crimes behind a veneer of algorithmic objectivity.

The same architecture extends beyond weapons. At 7amleh, we have documented how platforms suppress Palestinian speech, how state-linked actors use commercial platforms to shape information environments, and how Meta profits from content and accounts tied to illegal settlement expansion and violent rhetoric against Palestinians.

Two studies in Digital Domination make the point from different angles. One examines the Israeli government’s use of Google advertising to place its preferred narratives in front of people searching for information. Another examines algorithmic voice surveillance, showing how Palestinian speech itself is captured as data for systems of control.

This is where digital erasure becomes inseparable from physical violence. The destruction of Gaza also threatens the evidence and memory through which Palestinians can establish what was done to them. Platforms have removed or restricted documentation of Israeli violence, while physical archives, cultural records, cemeteries and the evidence beneath Gaza’s rubble have been destroyed or put at risk.

The UN refugee agency UNRWA ran a covert 10-month operation to smuggle millions of documents out of Gaza and East Jerusalem, amid fears that the originals, and even their digital copies, could be seized or destroyed. This September, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, warned that Israel’s clearance of Gaza’s rubble could destroy evidence of atrocity crimes, and called it unacceptable that Gaza’s reconstruction be conditioned on the erasure of its past and the evidence needed to secure justice for its victims.

The problem, therefore, goes far beyond whether a post stays online. It concerns who retains the power to document reality, preserve history and establish evidence after violence has taken place. We have described this wider process as platformicide: the destruction and denial of the digital spaces through which Palestinians communicate, organise, document and preserve collective memory.
Now the same problem is entering the systems through which people increasingly access knowledge.

Large language models and AI agents are becoming intermediaries between people and information, yet they are acutely vulnerable to manipulation. Microsoft’s security researchers have documented “AI recommendation poisoning,” in which companies embed hidden instructions that plant persistent biases in AI assistants’ memory, with 31 companies across 14 industries identified.

Salesforce researchers found that web-search agents fed authoritative-looking false content will reproduce it as fact: in controlled tests, around 80 percent of queries returned the attacker’s preferred answer, and in more realistic conditions, with poisoned documents buried among more than 100,000 clean ones, nearly one in four did.

For Palestine, this is not hypothetical. Drop Site News reported that Israel awarded a USD 46.5 million contract to Brad Parscale’s firm Clock Tower X to build networks of websites and blog posts aimed at shaping what chatbots tell users about Gaza, content written for machines rather than readers. Journalists have since put leading chatbots to the test to see how far the campaign has reached.

A society already subjected to censorship, propaganda, data extraction and the destruction of evidence is now entering an information environment in which people increasingly depend on AI systems to tell them what is true, what happened and what matters, and in which the party responsible for the violence is paying to shape those answers.

The danger is not only inaccurate information. It is the concentration of epistemic power in systems whose training data, retrieval mechanisms and decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Information manipulation can move from suppressing a Palestinian post to shaping what an AI system retrieves, remembers, or presents as knowledge.

Meanwhile, the technologies and companies enabling these systems are becoming embedded in public life elsewhere. In the UK, Palantir’s GBP 330 million National Health Service (NHS) contract led a parliamentary committee to call the company’s growing public-sector role “an unacceptable point of weakness”, and the government is now reviewing the contract amid pressure to use a break clause in 2027. In the United States, Amnesty International has documented how technology from Palantir and Babel Street is used to monitor and target migrants and people speaking out for Palestinian rights.

These developments should be understood as part of a wider transformation in how power is organised. Palestine shows what happens when data, surveillance infrastructure, artificial intelligence and corporate power are integrated into systems of domination. It also shows how quickly technologies developed in one context travel into another, stripped of the political conditions of their making and repackaged as innovation, efficiency, security or digital transformation.

The authoritarianism of the digital age does not require every state to build its own surveillance apparatus. It can purchase one. It does not require governments to control every source of information. It can outsource the infrastructure through which information is filtered, ranked and delivered. It does not require violence to disappear from public view. It can make violence more scalable, more automated and harder to attribute.
Palestinians are already living with the consequences. The rest of the world should heed the warning before these systems become too deeply embedded in its own institutions to challenge.

articles.title: When Big Tech becomes a tool of state control in Kenya
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them
Originally published on Global Voices
Image of person using Telegram by Christian Wiediger via Unsplash (Free to use). Image of Kenyan flag by User:Pumbaa80 via Wikimedia Commons(Public domain). Illustration by Global Voices.

This post by Grace Kobare is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On January 30, 2018, Raila Odinga held his symbolic “swearing-in” ceremony in Nairobi, and the government, through Kenya’s regulator, switched off the transmitters of KTN, NTV and Citizen TV while they were broadcasting live.
The Interior Ministry defended the move, saying the media had been given a security briefing in advance. The stations stayed off air for days and were only fully back by February 9, 2018.
Kenya's internet freedom drops drastically

The 2018 incident was just one of many examples of Kenyan officials cutting off connectivity — particularly during times of unrest. During the June 2024 tax protests, authorities shut down internet connectivity for around seven hours and arrested a large number of protesters. The Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) also reported that at least three networks blocked the web version of Telegram during those protests, and the blocks were reversed the same day.

A year later, during the June 2025 protests throughout Kenya, a communications authority issued a directive to media houses to stop live broadcasts of the unrest, and Telegram was blocked again. Access Now said this violated a High Court injunction against interfering with internet and Telegram access.

Given these incidents, it is no surprise that Kenya’s internet freedom record has worsened in recent years. Freedom House found that in 2025 Kenya had the most severe decline of the 72 countries assessed during the coverage period.
A wider pattern of internet freedom decline

Kenya’s experience is part of a wider pattern. Freedom House found that global internet freedom declined for the 15th consecutive year in 2025, as authoritarian governments used censorship and offline repression to crush protests organized online. Access Now’s 2025 report found that at least 313 shutdowns were implemented globally, and that in Africa the internet was shut down 30 times in 15 countries, with protests the leading trigger, followed by elections.

In Tanzania, an internet blackout was imposed after protests erupted on election day, October 29, 2025. It was only partially eased on November 4, alongside a curfew. An opposition lawyer said online mobilization was part of the reason for the blanket block, and protesters used VPNs to reach platforms such as X Spaces.

In Uganda, the regulator ordered all mobile operators and internet providers to suspend public internet access nationwide from 6 p.m. on 13 January 2026, two days before the general election. Officials had publicly denied plans for a blanket shutdown beforehand. The platforms themselves have been targets too: A Facebook ban followed the five-day blackout of the 2021 election and was still in effect in 2026, and Starlink disabled its terminals in the country after Uganda ordered the service shut down on grounds they were unlicensed.
Kenya’s case shows how state pressure on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them.
Checks through Kenya’s courts
The June 2025 Telegram block came despite a High Court injunction. The government has also tried to write that power into law.

In October 2025, President William Ruto signed the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act. Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it risks criminalizing legitimate online speech. The Act also expanded the powers of a state committee, the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4), to make websites and apps inaccessible.

The High Court in Nairobi suspended key sections a week after Ruto signed it. By July 2026, the High Court had declared the website-blocking powers unconstitutional. The chairperson of the Bloggers Association of Kenya, Kennedy Kachwanya, told Human Rights Watch that the amended law poses an unacceptable threat to digital rights and freedom of expression.
Beyond individual platforms

Amnesty International documented a coordinated campaign between June 2024 and July 2025 that used social media and digital tools to suppress Gen Z-led protests in Kenya. Amnesty found that X was central to pro-government networks, as pro-government actors posted identical messages repeatedly to hijack the platform’s algorithm and sway public perception. Amnesty noted that X failed to act on organized campaigns that violate its own policy. A participant told Amnesty he was part of a network of around 20 people paid roughly KES 25,000 (USD 192.50) to KES 50,000 (USD 385.29) a day to push pro-government messages onto X’s trending lists.

The Kenyan government is now seeking more direct leverage over big tech companies. The ICT Cabinet Secretary told the Senate that X must open a physical office in Kenya within three months or lose operating approval. The directive extends to TikTok and Meta, and gives the communications authority powers to suspend non-compliant platforms. The government framed this as a move to protect children online. However, a rights group summary of the move cautions that local presence could let authorities pressure staff and demand takedowns quietly.

Kenya’s courts have so far pushed back on some of the harshest measures, but the pressure keeps changing, from switching off television in 2018, to disrupting internet access in 2024 and blocking Telegram in 2025, and now to demands that platforms set up offices in the country.

What happens next depends partly on the companies themselves. They can resist orders that silence their users, or they can decide that keeping access to the Kenyan market is worth complying with the government’s demands. For Kenyans who rely on these platforms to organize and to be heard, that choice matters, because it helps decide how much of their public conversation stays free from state control.

articles.title: The problem with Shane Gillis’s joke isn’t just sexism, it’s sex work stigma
articles.author: Carmen Logie, Full Professor, Factor-Inwentash Faculty of Social Work, University of Toronto
paras: In his Oct. 10 Saturday Night Live (SNL) monologue, American comedian Shane Gillis joked that women at the gym dress like “whores” these days. The backlash was swift and widespread, in the news and across social media. Critics zeroed in on the sexualization of women who are simply trying to exercise without being harassed or judged.

While that’s fair, much of the criticism overlooked another problem. The objections often came down to this: these women aren’t sex workers, so they shouldn’t be called “whores.” That response leaves the insult itself intact, along with the assumption that being compared to a sex worker is degrading.

However well-intentioned, Canadian actor Dan Levy, for example, argued on Instagram only that wearing short shorts to the gym doesn’t make women “whores,” it makes the men calling them that misogynists.

The normalization of stigma toward sex workers runs deep. Everyday language, media coverage and public conversations all contribute to stigmatizing attitudes toward sex workers and to social norms that can fuel discrimination and exclusion. When we object to women being called “whores,” we can unintentionally reinforce the idea that being compared to a sex worker is an insult.
Gillis also joked about looking lesbian and gay, adding homophobia to the mix. Sex work stigma and homophobia have this in common: both are rooted in ideas of sexual immorality and deviance.
Stigma toward sex workers matters

Sex workers around the world experience profound health and social inequities. A recent series in The Lancet Public Health documents their disproportionate exposure to violence, unsafe working conditions and poor health outcomes. The series traces these sustained inequities to stigma and the criminalization of sex work.

Canada is no exception. Canada’s sex work laws, such as the Protection of Communities and Exploited Persons Act (PCEPA), criminalize purchasing sexual services even though selling one’s own sexual services generally is not.

This can make it harder for sex workers to screen potential clients because it limits how they can communicate with them and negotiate their safety. For instance, clients may be reluctant to share their identifying information due to fear of being arrested, in turn making it harder for sex workers to verify their identity, check references and learn about potentially dangerous clients.

Fear of police surveillance can also drive sexual transactions into more isolated settings, making it harder for sex workers to access help if needed. Criminalizing third-party involvement can also create barriers to safety arrangements, such as working with others to screen clients.
But why is calling a woman a “whore” still considered an insult?
Where the stigma comes from

In his 1963 book Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity, sociologist Erving Goffman described stigma as a social process through which certain people are labelled and discredited. Among them were people judged as “immoral,” like sex workers and lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer people.
But stigma is more than a set of negative attitudes. It’s also about power: who has access to resources and opportunities, who is valued and who is seen as deserving of dignity and respect.

Feminist scholar Gail Pheterson explored how this plays out for women in her work on “whore stigma” more than 30 years ago. She argued that the label “whore” is used to control women’s sexuality by sorting women into groups of those considered respectable and those judged immoral, dishonourable or sexually deviant.

It’s crucial to note that a woman does not even have to be a sex worker to be labelled a “whore.” Any woman perceived as violating gendered expectations of how to dress, act or express her sexuality can be.

This brings us back to Gillis’s joke. The women at the gym are not being called “whores” because their occupation is to sell sex. Gillis uses sex work as shorthand for sexual deviance. The joke only works if being compared to a sex worker is accepted as degrading. And this is the problem.

In other words, it is possible to challenge the sexism reflected in the policing of some women’s bodies and still overlook the gender-based stigma toward the women whose identities are being used as an insult.
The connection to homophobia

Gillis’s jokes about looking gay or lesbian draw on the same logic. While homophobia and stigma toward sex workers have distinct histories, both are rooted in social expectations about whose sexuality is considered acceptable.

Researchers call the devaluation of people based on same-gender attraction, identities, relationships and practices “sexual stigma.” It extends well beyond insults and negative attitudes. Sexual stigma shapes laws, health care, employment, opportunities and social relationships. It also limits people’s ability to live safely and openly, with dignity and full rights.
Multiple forms of stigma can also intersect. Queer sex workers, for example, may face stigma and discrimination related to both their sexual identity and their occupation.
Reclaiming a slur versus using one
A joke premised on the idea that being gay, lesbian or a sex worker is embarrassing or shameful does more than fall flat. It reproduces wider social beliefs about who’s acceptable and who’s not.

Interestingly, some sex workers have reclaimed the term “whore” to resist stigma and express pride. But there is a difference between a marginalized community reclaiming a stigmatizing label and outsiders using it to demean.
The backlash against Gillis’s SNL monologue raises an important question: can we challenge the policing of women’s bodies without reinforcing stigma toward sex workers?
We can — and we should. Women deserve to exercise without being sexualized, judged or harassed. Sex workers deserve the same dignity, safety and respect.

When we fight against women being called “whores,” we should ask whether we are mainly concerned because these women aren’t sex workers. This becomes a problem if it means accepting that a sex worker is someone unworthy of respect.
What we need to talk about more as a society is not just that women at the gym are being compared to sex workers. It’s that being compared to a sex worker continues to be used as an insult.

articles.title: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
articles.author: Paolo Stuppia, Sociologue, membre du CESSP (Centre Européen de Sociologie et de Science Politique), Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne
paras: Following widespread looting sprees and acts of violence occurring on the sidelines of the October 17 student protests, so-called “casseurs” seem to be the centre of attention. But the term, which comes from the French verb casser or “to break”, poses more questions than answers. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia examines the unprecedented situation many cities across France are having to contend with, and the complex combination of collective action whose motivations are unclear and the social media’s extreme agility.
The Conversation: How unprecedented are the scenes of looting that we witnessed on the sidelines of the October 17 demonstrations?

Paolo Stuppia: What may be unprecedented is the extent of the destruction of private property and the goods that have been stolen. It should be clear, however, that not all the looters can necessarily be sorted into identifiable groups, at least politically.

Indeed, as the politician Xavier Crettiez, the sociologist Isabelle Sommier and the historian François Audigier emphasised in 2021 in their joint project Violences politiques en France, the targets of acts of violence that are considered to be politically motivated can be determined both by technical constraints and the militant culture of the people involved. Let us recall Italy in the 1970s when autonomous activists spoke of “self-reduction” (the act of seizing goods or essential services), Maoists in France spoke of proletarian reappropriation. Their raid on Fauchon’s luxury grocery store on place de la madeleine and the redistribution of goods to slums and workers’ hostels that ensued went down in history as their biggest claim to fame.

Can we go as far as to say that the October 17 looting sprees were politically motivated? Even if we do not have all the details concerning the profiles of the people arrested, videos posted on social media and stolen goods being resold online tend to rule out the idea. That said, at least some of the targets were chosen haphazardly. While some are symbols of capitalism, like luxury stores, insurance companies, banks, multinationals, others included a number of more localised stores, small shops selling toys or video games; for example, which are rarely targets for such incidents.

If, especially since the alter-globalisation movement, we have seen the emergence of damage to property, primarily targeting symbols of capitalism and multinationals, in particular; this phenomenon goes hand in hand with “off the cuff” incidents by groups without any political affiliation, who join demonstrations to “get in on the act” in such a way that we are unable to determine whether it’s just a way of letting off steam or if it’s driven by a goal of redistributing goods – this weekend we witnessed some scenes of goods being redistributed, such as food being given to the homeless.
What do we know about casseurs’ profiles? When did they appear in the demonstrations and when did the term first appear in the media?

P.S.: Historically, the first research article on the casseur phenomenon can be traced back to the sociologist Gwenola Ricordeau. In France in the 1990s, as was the case during the student and high school movement of 1998, Ricordeau noticed that young people came to demonstrations to commit acts of vandalism or to mug people without having anything to do with the causes behind protest movements. They were driven by opportunism and also a desire to break up the monotony of everyday life.

The fact of disqualifying people by designating them as “criminals on the street” therefore ultimately leads us to riot-like phenomena, with or without the “looting” element, which are part of the continuity of “suburban revolt” or “city riots” which have gradually developed in working-class neighbourhoods since the second half of the 1970s. As we demonstrated alongside the sociologist Valérie Becquet in our book Géopolitique de la jeunesse, it forms a collection of pejorative and disqualifying terms pertaining to a so-called “dangerous youth”.

The term “casseur”, along with the derogatory term “racaille”, an old French term meaning rabble for example, widely resonated in the language of the media during the 2005 unrest to refer to a lumpenproletariat of young people who attacked both police and vandalised private property and a number of public services and property or street furniture, but whose actions were void of any political meaning.

If we take the theory of labelling, we can understand that the term “casseurs” is linked to the stigma attached to young people from working-class neighbourhoods. But there can also be a second meaning: the phenomena in which France’s Mouvance autonome (a movement drawing its influences from anarchism and situationism that sets itself apart), is involved in scenes of outbreaks of violence and damage to property, even harm targeting individuals. However, we should first note that the movement has a history of claiming responsibility for its actions. The casseur stigma is also turned around and sometimes used with self-derision.

In 2006, during the protests over contrat première embauche or first job contract law, there were tensions between those who said “we aren’t” or “we don’t want casseurs”, others who said, “it’s the government and the employers – they are the casseurs”. And it was in this context that a banner that appeared in Rennes (in western France), ended up in Paris, claiming: “We are all casseurs.” As if to recognise the term for what it is: a historically vague label, covering different realities, and that the media has invited to every protest movement without fail over the past 30 years.

It’s a bit like the expression “black bloc”: “casseurs” is used to refer to people who resort to techniques that are out of order or who conjure up a considerable cause for concern among a certain part of public opinion, and yet the term remains very vague and is easily instrumentalised.
How is social media a gamechanger for law enforcement?

P.S.: There is a clear difference between fairly structured protest movements, even in an informal way, and the much more spontaneous use of social networks to stage action among young and very young people, such as filming themselves wearing football shirts as they leave Paris’ Place de la République.

We are facing a generation that is demonstrating a certain digital agility. There is a proliferation of platforms. In the days of the yellow vests, we were still largely using tools that came from the Internet of the 2000s, whether it was Instagram, Facebook, a bit of messaging, but not that much, and also Twitter. What we are now seeing is a new wave of social networks in action, with tools also designed to reduce control, like Snapchat, or Telegram, where content is extremely short-lived.

The question would then be: how do we adapt to these new ways of using social media? There is also the phenomenon of loops, which are difficult to infiltrate, with people who move very quickly and provide real-time support for those involved in the movements, on a rather confidential level. One of the hypotheses would be that, in this case, law enforcement is a bit helpless.

There is a quickfire of information, several levels of conversation, with public and private chatrooms, and more or less restricted groups. These real-time conversations are much more difficult to apprehend. Beyond messages that rapidly disappear on Snapchat, for example, a whole set of parameters specific to this universe must be taken into account: profiles feature scores related to the person’s activity; anyone who infiltrates is therefore almost immediately identifiable.

The combination of extremely agile social media and protesters’ mobility is very difficult to control. An example of this was the youth movements in Hong Kong in 2019-2020, which caused a lot of trouble for the authorities, even though it involved a police force with a tutelary government that could still be called authoritarian. Even they struggled to control the groups of young demonstrators operating via social networks, committing fragmented acts, with ten people in one place, ten at another, dispersing quickly. It makes you wonder how much of an information time lapse we are contending with . But that will be up to the parliamentary commission of inquiry to work out.
Interview by Aurélie Djavadi.

articles.title: Africa’s bats could survive climate change – if they can find somewhere to live
articles.author: Mariëtte van der Walt, Biodiversity Coordinator, Wilderness, University of the Witwatersrand
paras: Climate change and changes in the way land is used are the two biggest threats to wildlife because they change the environment in which animals survive and thrive. Knowing how species respond to these pressures is central to planning conservation actions.
A number of studies have modelled how climate change will affect vertebrate distributions. But little is known about bats from tropical and subtropical regions, especially in Africa.

Bats are particularly sensitive to changes to their environment because of their slow reproductive rates, dependence on stable roosts, and sensitivity to climatic extremes that shape insect availability – their main source of food.

They therefore need both suitable foraging landscapes and the availability of caves for roosting. Research has been done on how bats will be affected by the effects of climate change such as rising temperatures. What has been overlooked is the fact that cave-dependent bats can’t survive in climatically suitable areas without access to suitable roosts.

So even if a future landscape has the right temperature and rainfall, it may be of little use to a bat if there is nowhere suitable to roost. That led us to a simple question: what happens when the places with the right climate aren’t the places with caves?

Having studied bats since 2017, I have spent much of my research career investigating their ecology and dependence on particular habitats. This experience led me to question where climate change might push wildlife. I wanted to understand whether Africa’s cave-dwelling bats would actually be able to find somewhere to live as the climate changes.

My co-author Mark Keith and I set out to answer this by building a model that brought together future climate conditions and the availability of caves and rocky roosting habitat across sub-Saharan Africa. We used cave-dwelling long-fingered bats called Miniopteridae as our study group to explore how these two essential pieces of the puzzle might overlap in the future.

Long-fingered bats are found widely across Africa and depend heavily on caves for shelter. They also commonly occur alongside other cave-dwelling bat species, making them a useful group for understanding how climate change could affect bats that rely on caves.

Our findings suggest that Africa’s cave-dwelling bats face a double challenge. Climate change could shrink the areas where they can live, but even where future conditions remain suitable, there might not be caves.
Places need to found where three things come together: the climate remains suitable; there is somewhere for the bats to live; and they can move between the places they need.
These could become critical safe havens for bats as the climate changes.
Modelling where bats can survive

We used an existing database of 551 reliable records showing where these bats have been found across sub-Saharan Africa. We then used these records to ask where conditions could remain suitable for them as the climate changes. Using a computer model, we matched each of these places with its local climate, such as how hot, cold or wet it gets, to work out what conditions the bats need. We then asked the model where those conditions would still exist around 2070, if the world carries on warming at a moderate rate.

We found that, depending on how the climate changes in the coming decades, the area with suitable conditions for these bats could shrink by 36% to 64% by 2061-2080. The areas that remained suitable were concentrated mainly in southern Africa, the eastern highlands and Madagascar.
We then went on to answer the next question. Were there caves in those places?

When we compared the areas with a suitable future climate with the locations of suitable caves and rocky landscapes, the picture became much more worrying. Only around 5% of the areas with suitable caves also had a climate expected to remain suitable for the bats. And when we considered how vulnerable the surrounding landscape was to future change, that fell to around 2%.
In other words, the places where bats might find the right climate and the places where they might find a home barely overlapped.

In addition, for some cave-dwelling bats, survival is not simply about finding one suitable cave. They may depend on a network of caves spread across the landscape, moving between them at different times of the year. That means the landscape between caves matters too.

A cave might provide an ideal shelter, but if the surrounding landscape has become heavily fragmented by roads, cities, agriculture or other changes, reaching another suitable cave may become much more difficult. And flying takes energy. If bats have to travel further between places where they can feed, rest and reproduce, they may have to spend more of their limited energy simply getting around. For animals already dealing with a changing climate, that could add another layer of pressure.
A problem that goes beyond bats

Our findings are important for a range of animals. A frog may need a particular wetland. A bird may depend on a particular type of forest. A plant may only grow in a certain kind of soil. As the climate changes, the conditions these species need may shift, but their homes may not.

This creates a challenge for conservation: it is not enough to ask where the climate will be suitable for wildlife in the future. We also need to ask whether wildlife will actually have somewhere to live when it gets there.

articles.title: Japan’s expensive funerals and declining birth rates are transforming ancestral traditions
articles.author: Mimi Hanaoka, Associate Professor of Religious Studies, University of Richmond
paras: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo’s Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals.
For generations, Japan’s funeral system rested on family and community networks and Buddhist temples. Together, they sustained the traditional system of burials into the 20th century.

Today, Japan is facing a crisis of funerals and burials. Funerals averaged approximately 1.2 million yen or about US$7,600, according to a 2024 national survey – approximately one-quarter of an average Japanese worker’s annual gross earnings.

Consequently, many Japanese are thinking about whether to continue burial traditions that will place on their children and grandchildren the financial, logistical and emotional costs associated with maintaining the family grave. Japan’s falling birthrate means there are fewer people to care for their ancestors’ graves, which has made the problem more urgent.

As a professor of religion who researches death rituals, I am struck by the innovative death rituals that are emerging in Japan, where I was born and raised. These new rituals reshape some traditions but preserve the importance of remaining connected with the dead.
Japanese funerary rites involve both cremation and burial. First the deceased is cremated, then their bones are buried, typically weeks, months or years after cremation.
Cremation is overwhelmingly standard for Japanese burials today, with between 99.7% and 99.9% of the deceased cremated. In any given year, fewer than 400 people are buried without cremation.

After the deceased is cremated in a coffin, family members place some or most of the bone fragments into a funerary urn. Family members take the urn home to be placed on a Buddhist altar. The bones are later interred in a grave, ossuary or columbarium – “nōkotsudō” – which are permanent structures where bones are interred in compartments.

Traditionally, mourners at Japanese funerals bring a cash gift to offset the cost of funerals. Protocol dictates that the family of the deceased later send return gifts that are worth half the value of the cash gift that was given. These are typically gift boxes of coffee or tea, or elegant but pragmatic items, such as high-quality towels or soaps, sent within a few weeks of the funeral.
Post-death Buddhist rituals are held weekly through the 49th day and then continue periodically, at minimum, until the third death anniversary.

The price for a grave and interment are in addition to the funeral costs. Purchasing a grave means buying the headstone and use of the plot; the temple, municipal cemetery or private cemetery owns the land itself.

In 2025, a gravestone, plot and cemetery-use fees amounted to 1.52 million yen – close to $10,000. The combined costs of an average funeral and average grave are equivalent to almost 60% of of an average worker’s annual salary.

Costs do not end after cremation, funeral and burial. Municipal and private cemeteries charge annual fees for land maintenance. There are additional fees for Buddhist rituals to be performed at the grave, which are believed to benefit the deceased in the afterlife.

Most Tokyo municipal cemeteries charge less than $40 per year. These costs fall on descendants, who also traditionally visit and maintain the grave, make offerings and keep the grave and surrounding area neat and tidy.

Graves can be effectively repossessed by the cemetery or temple if they are abandoned and annual maintenance fees go unpaid. The bones in a repossessed grave are then reinterred in a communal ossuary or columbarium.
Tree burials and other adaptations
The combination of a shrinking population, limited grave plots and costs that continue in perpetuity make alternatives to a traditional grave attractive.

These include “tree burials,” known as “jumokusō,” where the deceased’s bones or ashes are buried in or around a tree. Tree burials are becoming increasingly popular, with a 2022 consumer survey indicating that they account for just over 40% of all new graves.

Two Tokyo Metropolitan public cemeteries now offer “Forest Type” – “Jūrin-gata” – burial, where cremated remains in silk bags are interred into a designated plot of land. A living individual can reserve a burial spot and know that there will be no management fees in perpetuity.

This is in contrast to regular Tokyo Metropolitan public cemeteries’ graves, for which an individual cannot reserve a spot while still alive. Grave plots are first-come, first-served, and since death is unpredictable, graves cannot be reserved in advance.

Some opt for ossuaries and columbariums, which exist in various styles, from more traditional Buddhist altar-style compartments to modern locker-style housing for the urns. There are even automated columbariums, where urns are stored in a centralized system and then retrieved mechanically and placed in a private memorial cubby when a family visits to pay respects to their loved ones. There are also communal ossuaries, where the deceased’s bones are mixed with the bones of others, either immediately or after a certain period of time.
Bone buddhas and other innovations

Arrestingly beautiful but rare are the bone buddhas – “kotsubotoke” – statues of Amida Buddha, or Buddha of Infinite Light. They are made from the partial remains of tens and sometimes hundreds of thousands of individuals’ cremated remains that have been pulverized into fine ash before being compressed into sculptures.

Amida Buddha is especially important for Japanese death practices. Devotion to the Amida Buddha is associated with a good death and rebirth in the Pure Land, a domain believed to be conducive to attaining buddhahood and enlightenment.

Historically, these bone buddhas were a creative innovation that offered a beautiful solution for temples with a difficult problem: what to do with the bones left in their care of those who had nobody to claim their remains, such as the poor, travelers and foreigners.

Today, the few temples that offer this rare practice accept full or partial bones – even just several grams of bones – which are collected and held at the temple until there are sufficient bones to construct a bone buddha.

Others opt for “hakajimai,” or grave-closing, in which the urns buried in a family grave are disinterred and the bones are reinterred elsewhere, such as a communal ossuary. Abandoned and neglected graves are seen as a blight – emblematic of the collapse of the traditional family system of caring for the dead. The process of “hakajimai” ends the family’s responsibility for maintaining the family grave and paying regular dues.
People opt for “hakajimai” because it ends the logistical, financial and emotional costs of maintaining the family grave and does not pass on those burdens to the next generation.
How the living interact with the dead
In Japan, the dead remain part of the social worlds of the living. Family relationships and ritual obligations maintain the connections of the dead and the living across generations.

Traditional rituals are becoming difficult to sustain. Nevertheless, people are still finding ways to remain connected to the dead. Changing burial practices is one way in which people are reshaping old traditions to accommodate modern demands.

articles.title: Built for boats, adrift on land: Bangladesh’s Bede community struggles with a fixed-address system
articles.author: Masudul Zarif
paras: ‘We cannot change the river, and we cannot stop moving’
Originally published on Global Voices
Boats and people on the Turag River, Dhaka, Bangladesh. Image via Flickr by Wonderlane. CC BY 2.0.

For nomadic Bede families on the Jamuna River in central Bangladesh, moving is a routine part of life. A study published in May 2026 in the journal Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health looked at three nomadic settlements in Tangail district of central Bangladesh: Jugiyar Char, Palima and Char Nikrail. It found that these families move several times a year, driven by seasonal floods and erosion, as well as searches for paying audiences. However, climate change and increasingly unpredictable river conditions are forcing these communities to land.

The researchers conducted a micro-case study through 12 interviews and one focus group during Bangladesh’s 2025 monsoon season (June through October). It describes displacement as an ongoing condition, not a single event. “We cannot change the river, and we cannot stop moving,” one sardar, or community leader, told them.

A second study, published online in August 2026 in Dhaka University’s Social Science Review, highlights the dire environmental exposure and disaster vulnerabilities of Bede settlements in Munshiganj, calling for organized cooperation between government agencies and relief NGOs.

The Bede are a traditionally mobile community that has lived and worked on Bangladesh’s rivers for generations. They have long been marginalized in Bangladeshi society, and many make a living as snake charmers, folk healers, sellers of herbal medicine and amulets, and street performers.

Historical accounts often trace the community’s roots to 1638, when groups arrived in Dhaka alongside the exiled king of Myanmar’s northwestern coastal region (then Arakan). It is difficult to get an accurate count of how many Bede exist in Bangladesh today. Climate Watch, a Bangladeshi news site, has cited figures ranging from about 75,000, from the Department of Social Services, to roughly 800,000.
Families traditionally travel in boat groups led by a sardar (leader). When they stop on land, they often camp on riverbanks or on chars, the sandbars that big rivers build up and wash away.

This is not ordinary migration. Researchers from the study published in Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health contrast it with refugees who flee a single event: Bede families are almost always on the move, which makes them hard to reach for clinics, schools, and civil registers that assume a fixed address.
Today, many of these families are being forced to move away from their river roots and are settling on land.

Community members share that climate change has forced many to give up on the river as worsening floods, erosion, and storms make their former settlements uninhabitable. They also said some canals and channels are drying up, making life on the water impossible in some areas.

In terms of income, one sardar explained that families stay about a month in one place and leave when audiences stop coming. In Munshiganj, respondents told the Dhaka University team that demand for traditional work is falling, that stigma pushes people away from it, and that a recent ban on snake-catching has cost them income. About 88 percent said they did not want their children to follow the traditional trades.

Concerning work on land, in 2019, leaders of the Bede settlement in Savar, near Dhaka, one of the country’s largest, told a police officer that poverty and dying rivers meant families could no longer sail to other areas, and that interest in snake-charming and other old trades was fading.

To expand Bede people’s economic opportunities, the Uttaran Foundation, a local NGO, has trained about 200 young Bede women, who now work in garment factories. While both aforementioned studies are hyper-local and may not apply to all settlements, they reflect a tension between modern life, environmental realities, and traditions.
Services built for people who stay put
The Dhaka University study notes that many Bede families are landless and lack official citizenship documents, which limits their access to relief and disaster programs.

Part of the problem is simple logistics. In Bangladesh, official papers are tied to a fixed address, and many Bede families don’t have one. The Red Cross Red Crescent Magazine noted in 2023 that because the Bede usually live in temporary settlements and “don’t have permanent addresses,” getting the ID cards and other documents needed for basic services becomes impossible. The gap runs deeper than paperwork, though. Legal researcher Tamanna Tabassum Kabir wrote in the Indraprastha Law Review in 2020 that the Bede are not listed as an ethnic group in the national census, and that they “have not been officially recognized as citizens” even though they have lived in Bangladesh for centuries.

Kabir writes that Bede people could not enroll as voters until 2008. That mattered beyond the ballot box. According to a Canadian immigration board report, the government issued national ID cards using data collected for voter registration, so getting on the voter list was a way into other documents. The door hasn’t fully opened, though. In 2019, Philip Gain reported in The Daily Star, a local news outlet, that many Bede households own no land or house where they could be registered as voters.

A 2026 report by Bangladesh’s statistics bureau and the UN’s Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) found that children from smaller ethnic communities, and from families that have recently moved, are among the least likely to have their births registered.

United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) described what that looks like in Aftabnagar, in eastern Dhaka, during the 2023 Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign. The girls in the local Bede community had no birth certificates, so they could not be registered in the usual way. Kamrun Nahar, a vaccinator appointed by the Dhaka North City Corporation, spent many hours winning over the community leader and families, and visited at night, when everyone was home. The girls were eventually enlisted by hand. All 24 girls in the community received the vaccine in a single day, UNICEF reported in April 2024.

Some schools have tried to follow the families. An Ashoka profile of fellow A.K.M. Maksud describes six boat schools that traveled with Bede fleets near Dhaka, plus a fixed school in Aminbazar, run through his non-profit organization, Grambangla Unnayan Committee.
Adapting, not only enduring

The Cambridge study also documents how families manage the move. They negotiate with landowners and local youth before they settle, lean on a reputation built on earlier visits, and share food, money, and care within the group. Asked what would help improve their lives, participants named modest things: a small plot to live on, some help with work, medicine, and schools. The authors recommend mobile, community-based support designed with community leaders, not clinic-only models.
A 55-year-old Bede woman interviewed for the Munshiganj study said the younger generation no longer wants to live on boats and hopes education will help remove the stigma of being Bede.

Field observations from riverbank settlements in Savar, near Dhaka, highlight how these practical struggles play out. “Our ancestors lived and died on boats, but the rivers are no longer what they used to be,” observed Alamgir Sardar, a community leader in the area. “Without a permanent address on land, our children cannot get birth certificates or regular schooling. Moving to land is no longer a choice for us, as it is a matter of survival.”

For parents, the transition is also driven by hopes of breaking historical stigma. “I never went to school because we were always moving from one river ghāt to another,” shared Rahela Begum, a mother living in a temporary land settlement in Savar. “I want my children to study and live with dignity on land so they do not have to face the disrespect we experienced.”

articles.title: How a civic tech platform is helping women in Serbia get home safely
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: ‘[W]hat can we change in the spaces where people live, work, study and spend their free time?’
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from SafeSteps website. Caption reads in English: ‘Report approximate location anonymously — we see patterns, not identities,’ used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

For many women and girls in Serbia, safety is not only a question of physical protection. It influences their freedom of movement, their choices, and their ability to participate equally in public life. This issue cannot be viewed separately from the broader social position of women and young people. Reports by the Youth Umbrella Organisation of Serbia (KOMS) show that many young people experience insecurity, declining trust in institutions, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation in decisions that affect their lives. The reports also document concerning cases of pressure, threats, and security risks faced by young activists who publicly advocate for social change.

At the same time, reports of the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality highlight that gender-based discrimination and unequal treatment remain persistent challenges in Serbian society, affecting women and girls in various aspects of their everyday lives. Many incidents of harassment, intimidation, or discomfort in public spaces never become official complaints. Some women do not believe reporting will lead to change. Others fear judgment, social stigma, or consider their experience too minor to be important — but no experience is too small when it concerns the right to dignity, freedom of movement, and equal access to public spaces.

Global Voices conducted an email interview with Varvara Lazarevic, the head of an NGO in Novi Sad, Serbia, to find out what can be done about this universal problem. The NGO, Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad, and their project, SafeSteps, a civic technology platform where women can anonymously share their experiences of insecurity in public spaces, are presented here as an Impact Spotlight for the Serbian edition of the Digital Sparks Program.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Varvara Lazarevic (VL): Omladina JAZAS Novi Sad has been working with young people and different marginalized groups for many years, with a focus on improving quality of life through education, information and support. We founded Omladinske novine, a youth media outlet with both print and online editions, and since last year, we have also had our own podcast studio, where we work with young people and teach them about journalism, social media and media production. Digital Sparks was important to us because it gave us the opportunity to connect areas we have been working on for years — communication, human rights and youth work — with technology. and turn them into a practical tool. This is how Safe Steps was created. The idea had been developing for years through my professional work, research and work with young people and women. I wanted to explore how technology could become genuinely useful to people and give visibility to experiences that often remain unheard.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VL: For a long time, I had been thinking about experiences that happen every day but rarely become part of any official record. Someone changes the route home, walks faster through a certain part of town, sends a message to say they have arrived safely, or simply starts avoiding a particular place. All of these experiences tell us something about how people actually experience public space. When we talk about safety, the focus often falls on what individuals should do to protect themselves. I wanted to ask a different question: what can we change in the spaces where people live, work, study and spend their free time? SafeSteps grew out of that question. It gives people a way to anonymously share their experiences and mark the places where they happened. One experience can point to a problem, while several experiences can reveal a pattern. That can open a conversation with the community and institutions about what could be changed.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

VL: The most important thing we did was turn an idea into a functioning platform. SafeSteps is now live, and people can share their experiences and mark places where they experienced violence, harassment, discrimination or felt unsafe. Privacy was one of our main principles from the beginning. The platform works anonymously, without registration or the need to provide a name, email address or phone number. Locations are shown approximately, so that an experience can be connected to a public space while personal privacy remains protected. At the same time, we started building communication around the platform through social media and media outreach, explaining how SafeSteps works and encouraging people to share their experiences. Another important part of the platform is a network of more than 20 support contacts, where people can find information about different forms of assistance.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

VL: I think the most important change is that we have created another way for people to make their experiences visible. There are experiences that someone may want to share, but they also need a space where they feel safe and have control over the information they provide. SafeSteps offers exactly that. A person can share an experience anonymously and, at the same time, contribute to a broader picture of how people experience public space. For the young people we work with, the project is also a concrete example of how technology can be used for much more than communication and entertainment. It can be a tool for participation and for starting conversations about issues that affect their everyday lives. We are still at an early stage, so I think it is important to be realistic about long-term impact. For now, we are focused on understanding the experiences being shared and seeing how they can contribute to conversations about possible changes.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed through your participation in the project?

VL: I was already working at the intersection of communication, media, human rights and new technologies before this project. However, SafeSteps made me look at technology much more concretely as part of civic space. I became especially aware of the role of trust. When you ask people to share sensitive experiences, the way technology is designed becomes just as important as the idea behind it. Privacy, data protection and digital security are not only technical issues. They directly affect whether people feel comfortable participating. I also learned to think more carefully about the whole journey of information — from the moment a person shares an experience, through the way it is protected and processed, to how it can eventually support communication, research or dialogue with institutions. For me, this is an important part of digital democracy: creating practical and trustworthy ways for people to participate in the communities they are part of.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

VL: One of the most important things I have learned is that technology itself is not the solution. It becomes meaningful when it responds to a real need and is designed responsibly. Another important lesson is about privacy. When working with sensitive experiences, data protection has to be considered from the very beginning. People’s trust is built through every part of the platform. The experience of collaboration that Digital Sparks brought was also very valuable to me. I saw how much knowledge exists among organizations working on similar issues and how much we can learn from one another. And perhaps the most important lesson is that one voice can start a conversation. Several voices can reveal a pattern. Once a problem becomes visible, there is an opportunity to talk about how it can be addressed.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

VL: For me, SafeSteps is not a finished project. It is a beginning. We want to continue promoting the platform, follow how people use it and carefully look at the experiences that come in. It is important for us to understand which issues and locations stand out and how we can respond through dialogue with the community and institutions. I would like to strengthen cooperation with organizations, schools, universities, media and institutions that can contribute to safer and more inclusive public spaces. In the longer term, I see potential for the model to grow beyond Novi Sad and connect experiences from other cities in Serbia. We will also bring what we have learned through Digital Sparks into our wider work with young people. Through Omladinske novine and our podcast studio, we can continue to have conversations about digital rights, privacy, responsible technology and information. I would like us one day to be able to look at Serbia through citizens’ experiences and see both where problems exist and where progress has been made. For me, that is the real meaning of SafeSteps: making experiences visible, turning visibility into dialogue, and dialogue into change.
